purpose: Decide how a local CCTV-and-cloud-recording operator productizes cameras, cloud storage and support into lawful, honestly-sold subscription tiers: which segments to target first, whether to build on a white-label VSaaS platform or an own stack, how hardware, install and subscription margins interact as mechanisms, and what retention, access and contract promises the offer may make.
assumptions: no observed dataset supplied; all scores are heuristic priors
the operator is an own-build local installer-operator selling under its own brand, not an agent or franchisee of a major security company
revenue is a one-time installation charge plus a recurring per-site monthly subscription bundling cloud recording, camera support and footage help
all monetary quantities are expressed as mechanisms or qualitative bands and are verified per deal against current vendor rate cards and local win/loss evidence, never asserted as market fact
surveillance is sold only for lawful, disclosed purposes: deterrence, detection and evidence for the property owner
video privacy, audio-recording consent and camera-placement rules vary sharply by jurisdiction, so every design and proposal carries a verify-current-rules-in-your-jurisdiction flag
exclusions: site survey, coverage design, camera selection and placement, edge/cloud/hybrid recording architecture and its bandwidth and storage engineering math, camera network segmentation and hardening, cabling and commissioning tests - the camera system design and installation KB owns these

running the recurring service: camera-health monitoring, storage and retention operations, incident retrieval workflow, privacy signage and consent operations, viewer access audit, renewal handling and churn management - the cloud video operations and privacy compliance KB owns these
covert or unlawful surveillance products, hidden-camera requests, or advice on monitoring people without disclosure - such requests are declined, never designed or priced
asserting specific per-camera prices, subscription rates, market sizes or crime statistics as fact - only pricing mechanisms and qualitative bands with per-deal local verification
personalized legal, financial, tax or insurance advice - jurisdictional obligations are named as classes with a verify-locally flag, and buyers are directed to local counsel for specifics

competency_questions.question: What exactly does this business sell, and why is the per-site subscription rather than the camera hardware the asset being built?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: OFFER_THESIS states the deterrence/detection/evidence outcome, the two revenue events, and the subscription book as the compounding asset

competency_questions.question: What lawful-use boundaries constrain who the operator sells to and how surveillance may be framed, and how is a covert-intent buyer handled?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: LAWFUL_SURVEILLANCE_CHARTER names the disclosed-purpose rule, the jurisdiction-varying obligation classes with the verify-locally flag, and DISCOVERY_AND_QUALIFICATION shows the declared-purpose capture and the scripted decline

competency_questions.question: Which customer segments exist for camera-plus-cloud subscriptions, and how should a new operator choose the one or two to lead with?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SEGMENT_MAP gives per-segment loss profiles, buying triggers and fee tolerance, and BEACHHEAD_SELECTION applies repeatability, density and referral tests to pick 1-2 lead segments

competency_questions.question: When should the operator build on a white-label VSaaS platform versus running an own stack, and what must be verified about a platform vendor before signing?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: VSAAS_VS_OWNSTACK states the volume/engineering/capital mechanism and crossover framing, and PLATFORM_VENDOR_DILIGENCE lists license metering, white-label depth, camera openness, exit portability and vendor stability checks

competency_questions.question: What drives the monthly cost of serving a subscribed site, and how is each driver verified before a quote?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: COGS_MECHANICS enumerates storage, license, support labor, billing and reserve drivers with what moves each and its current verification source

competency_questions.question: How should subscription tiers be structured, and why must retention and access promises appear on the tier sheet itself?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: TIER_ARCHITECTURE gives the three-tier ladder with buyer-felt differentiators, and RETENTION_ACCESS_POLICY_IN_OFFER shows retention days, viewer roles, export handling and operator-access limits as priced product

competency_questions.question: How does the operator choose between hardware markup and hardware subsidy, and what must a subsidy always be matched to?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: HARDWARE_MARGIN_STRATEGY explains both allocations as mechanisms, the ownership-model consequences, and the rule that subsidy depth is covered by a term commitment

competency_questions.question: How is the installation job priced so the quote survives scrutiny, and how may install price interact with the subscription commitment?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: INSTALL_PRICING_MECHANISM shows the build-up from crew-day rate, difficulty factors and contingency, the one-time versus monthly separation, and the computed term-funded discount trade

competency_questions.question: How is each tier's monthly price set between a computed cost floor and a locally-tested value ceiling without ever asserting an invented market rate, and how do unit economics decide whether a deal is accepted?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SUBSCRIPTION_PRICE_SETTING gives the floor computation and local ceiling test, and UNIT_ECONOMICS_DASHBOARD gives site margin, payback and expected-life mechanisms with deal thresholds

competency_questions.question: What makes a contract term, renewal and exit design honest, and what must the contract say about footage and hardware when a customer leaves?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: CONTRACT_TERM_DESIGN covers term-to-subsidy matching, the auto-renewal notice obligation class with the verify-locally flag, and plain-language footage-and-hardware disposition on exit

competency_questions.question: How does the operator sell surveillance ethically - disclosure-first, without fear-mongering or capability inflation, and with care for vulnerable buyers - and how does the proposal make that visible?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: ETHICAL_SELLING_CODE states the written code with its four prohibitions and safeguards, and PROPOSAL_AND_QUOTE_STRUCTURE shows total-cost-over-term disclosure and the 2-3 option format

competency_questions.question: How does the offer position against DIY consumer cameras, alarm-company bundles, no-recurring installers and doing nothing?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: COMPETITIVE_POSITIONING names each alternative's honest gap and the operator's verifiable service-and-evidence difference without fear appeals

competency_questions.question: How are the first pilot and reference sites landed and converted without anchoring the market on discounts or misusing customer footage?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PILOT_AND_REFERENCE_SITES shows time-boxed pilot agreements with conversion dates, consented case-study mechanics and de-identification of bystanders

competency_questions.question: What must a closed deal hand to system design and to service operations before anything is scheduled, and on what triggers is the offer itself re-examined?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: HANDOFF_TO_DESIGN_AND_OPS defines the rejectable handoff package and its definition-of-done, and OFFER_GOVERNANCE_AND_REPRICE gives the trigger-driven review, reprice and grandfathering discipline

glossary.definition: Video-surveillance-as-a-service: a vendor-hosted cloud platform for recording, mobile apps and camera-health tooling that an operator licenses per camera or per site and resells, instead of building and running its own cloud.

A VSaaS resale arrangement where the operator's brand appears on the apps, portal and invoices while the vendor's platform runs underneath; its depth varies by vendor and determines who the customer thinks they bought from.

Recurring monthly revenue: the per-site subscription income that makes the book valuable; trade buyers price books as multiples of RMR, but any multiple is negotiated per transaction and never assumed as a fixed figure.
The number of days recorded footage is kept before overwrite; simultaneously a tier differentiator buyers feel and a direct cloud-storage cost driver, so it is always priced, never gifted.

Cloud storage of clips around motion or analytic events rather than a continuous stream; an honest tier lever that cuts storage cost, whose engineering configuration belongs to the system-design discipline.
Selling cameras and switches at or below cost and recovering the gap through subscription margin; financeable only when matched to a term commitment long enough to repay the gap.
The per-site monthly cost stack (storage, license, support labor, billing, reserve) plus target margin; the computed line below which a subscription price loses money on every month it is paid.

The highest monthly amount a segment credibly pays given its alternative set (DIY kits, alarm bundles, no-recurring installers, doing nothing); discovered locally through discovery and win/loss, never asserted from folklore.

Open camera interoperability standards; a platform that accepts ONVIF/RTSP devices preserves the operator's camera choice and exit options, while a captive hardware list couples the camera margin to the vendor.
Letting existing subscribers keep their current price or terms for a stated period after a reprice, with any later move made through the contract's notice mechanics rather than silently.

nodes.definition: Fix what the business actually sells: not cameras, but a per-site surveillance outcome - deterrence at entrances and yards, detection of incidents, and retrievable evidence for the property owner - delivered as an installed camera system plus a monthly cloud-recording-and-support subscription. The thesis states the two revenue events (a one-time install charge and a recurring per-site fee bundling cloud storage, system support and footage help), names the subscription book as the asset being built, and commits the offer to lawful, disclosed surveillance so every downstream platform, pricing and selling choice serves a compounding recurring-revenue book rather than one-off box sales.

included: the subscription book as the compounding asset

pros.claim: Anchoring on a per-site subscription outcome turns each install into a compounding revenue asset instead of a one-time job
pros.example: the operator who closes a taqueria at install-plus-monthly keeps earning from that site for years while the box-sale competitor re-hunts for work every month

cons.claim: An outcome-and-subscription framing loses buyers who only want cameras mounted cheaply once
cons.example: a homeowner who wants two cameras hung with no monthly fee walks away when every package includes a subscription

failure_modes: selling hardware jobs with the subscription tacked on as an optional afterthought, so the book never compounds
framing the product as watching people rather than protecting the buyer's property, inviting unlawful use cases into the pipeline
acceptance_tests: the one-page thesis states the outcome sold, both revenue events, the subscription book as the asset, and the lawful-disclosed-purpose commitment
revisit_triggers: repeated buyer pushback shows the outcome framing misses what a target segment actually buys
the money model itself changes, e.g. operator-owned hardware-as-a-service replaces customer-owned kit

base.update_signal: the outcome framing or the install-plus-subscription revenue model is restated

nodes.definition: Bind every offer, pitch and contract to lawful, disclosed surveillance serving the property owner's deterrence, detection and evidence needs. The charter forbids covert-monitoring products and pitches - no hidden-camera items, no undisclosed employee or tenant monitoring, no cameras aimed into a neighbor's private space - and names the obligation classes that vary sharply by jurisdiction: video surveillance of private areas, audio-recording consent (frequently stricter than video), workplace-monitoring disclosure, and camera-placement limits near sensitive zones. Because these rules differ by country, state and even city, every design and proposal carries an explicit verify-current-rules-in-your-jurisdiction flag instead of an asserted legal conclusion, and audio stays off by default until a local consent check clears it.

excluded: asserting any jurisdiction's specific rule as fact

pros.claim: A bright-line lawful-use charter protects the license to operate and screens out the deals most likely to end in liability
pros.example: declining a bar owner who wants a concealed camera near the staff changing area costs one deal and avoids a career-ending case

cons.claim: Hard boundaries and verify-locally caveats slow some sales and concede a few deals to less scrupulous competitors
cons.example: a buyer who wants audio on every camera today may leave rather than wait for a local consent-rule check

failure_modes: treating legality as an install-crew detail instead of an offer-design constraint baked into tiers and proposals
asserting a remembered legal rule as fact instead of flagging local verification
acceptance_tests: every proposal template carries the disclosed-purpose statement, the audio-off default and the verify-locally flag, and covert-use requests have a scripted refusal
revisit_triggers: a jurisdiction where the operator sells changes its video, audio or workplace-monitoring rules
a sales conversation surfaces a use case the charter does not clearly classify

base.update_signal: a surveillance, audio-consent or workplace-monitoring rule changes in a served jurisdiction

nodes.definition: Map the five workable segments - retail shops, restaurants, contractors' yards and job sites, small industrial premises, and residential - by what each loses without cameras and what triggers a purchase: retail buys after shrinkage or a break-in and wants entrance and till coverage; restaurants buy for dispute resolution plus back-door and register coverage; contractors buy after tool or material theft from yards and open sites; small industrial buys perimeter, loading-dock and liability documentation; residential buys package-theft reassurance. For each segment record the typical decision-maker, camera-count band, tolerance for a monthly fee, and where the buying trigger is heard (a police report, an insurer conversation, a neighbor's incident) - the map that tiers, pricing and pitches specialize against.

pros.claim: Segment-specific loss language makes discovery and tiering concrete instead of generic security talk
pros.example: walking a contractor through last winter's stolen-generator loss converts better than reciting a camera features list

cons.claim: Loss-profile stereotypes mislead on atypical sites inside a segment
cons.example: a boutique holding high-value stock behaves like small industrial on perimeter needs, not like typical retail

failure_modes: pitching one generic offer at all five segments and specializing nothing
building the map from imagination instead of local win/loss and incident conversations
acceptance_tests: each segment entry names its loss profile, buying trigger, decision-maker, camera-count band and monthly-fee tolerance
revisit_triggers: win/loss reviews contradict a segment's assumed trigger or fee tolerance
a new segment such as churches or schools shows repeat inbound demand

base.update_signal: local win/loss or incident evidence contradicts a mapped segment assumption

nodes.definition: Choose the one or two segments the young business leads with, using repeatability tests rather than taste: how similar sites are within the segment (a standard four-to-eight-camera restaurant kit installs faster every time), how dense the local cluster is (route density cuts truck-roll cost), how connected the owners are (restaurant and contractor owners refer within their trade), and how tolerant the segment is of a monthly fee. The choice concentrates the first pilots, the first tier sheet and the first reference stories on a market that can compound through referrals, while explicitly deferring the other segments instead of serving all of them badly.

included: repeatability, density, referral and fee-tolerance tests

pros.claim: A beachhead makes every install more like the last, compressing quote-to-commission time and error rate
pros.example: after five taquerias the crew pre-builds the same mount-and-switch kit and quotes the sixth in a single visit

cons.claim: Focus defers real revenue in other segments and can anchor the brand narrowly
cons.example: being known as the restaurant-camera company makes the first industrial-yard deal harder to win

failure_modes: chasing every inbound lead across all segments and standardizing nothing
picking a beachhead on personal familiarity instead of density and referral structure
acceptance_tests: the beachhead memo names 1-2 lead segments with the repeatability, density, referral and fee-tolerance evidence behind the choice and states what is deferred
revisit_triggers: pilot conversion in the chosen beachhead underperforms while another segment pulls inbound demand
the local market shifts, e.g. a franchise dealer sweeps the restaurant cluster

base.update_signal: pilot conversion or inbound-demand evidence contradicts the beachhead choice

nodes.definition: Decide whether the cloud layer is bought or built: a white-label VSaaS platform (the operator resells a vendor's cloud recording, apps and health tooling under a per-camera or per-site license) versus an own stack (the operator runs its own recording servers or self-hosted video management with storage it controls). Treat it as mechanism, not brand preference: the platform route trades a recurring license out of every subscription for near-zero engineering, fast launch, finished mobile apps and someone else's uptime problem; the own-stack route trades engineering payroll, on-call liability and slower launch for control of the whole margin and the roadmap. The decision hinges on subscribed-camera volume (license fees scale linearly while own-stack costs step), in-house engineering capability, capital patience and appetite for operational risk - and it is revisited at modeled volume thresholds, not annually by habit.

included: volume, engineering and capital decision drivers
excluded: designing the recording architecture per site

pros.claim: Starting on a proven VSaaS platform lets a two-person shop sell enterprise-grade cloud recording in week one
pros.example: white-labeling an established platform delivers finished mobile apps and camera-health alerts no small operator could build in a year

cons.claim: Every subscribed camera pays the platform forever, and switching later means touching every customer site
cons.example: a mature 300-camera book still sends a slice of each month's revenue to the vendor, and migrating means re-provisioning hundreds of devices

failure_modes: building an own stack first for engineering pride and drowning in operations before revenue exists
treating the platform license as free margin and never modeling the crossover
acceptance_tests: a decision memo records the chosen route, the volume/engineering/capital mechanism behind it, and the crossover conditions that would trigger re-evaluation
revisit_triggers: subscribed-camera volume crosses the modeled crossover band
the vendor's terms, pricing structure or ownership change materially

base.update_signal: subscribed volume, engineering capacity or vendor terms cross the decision memo's stated conditions

nodes.definition: Before white-labeling, interrogate the platform vendor the way a landlord reads a lease: how the license is metered (per camera, per site, per resolution or retention band) and what wholesale-versus-suggested-retail spread it leaves the operator; how deep the white-label goes (operator's brand on apps and portal, or the vendor's brand in front of the operator's customers); which cameras it accepts (open ONVIF/RTSP devices versus a captive hardware list that couples camera margin to the vendor); what happens at exit - whether footage, configurations and customer accounts export, and whether the cameras survive a platform change; and how stable the vendor itself is (funding, acquisition risk, and channel conflict from vendor-direct sales). The diligence sheet doubles as the negotiation agenda and the escape plan.

excluded: camera model selection for a site
negotiating specific rates in this KB

pros.claim: Exit-path diligence done before signing preserves the operator's book as the operator's asset rather than the vendor's
pros.example: choosing a platform that supports standard ONVIF cameras means a future migration re-points devices instead of replacing them on every ladder

cons.claim: Deep diligence delays launch and can over-weight risks a small book will never hit
cons.example: spending weeks comparing enterprise portability clauses while the first ten customers wait is beachhead time wasted

failure_modes: signing for the demo experience without reading how the license is metered
discovering channel conflict only when the vendor's direct sales team quotes the operator's own prospect
acceptance_tests: the diligence sheet answers license metering, white-label depth, camera openness, data/exit portability and vendor stability with evidence, and names the walk-away conditions
revisit_triggers: the vendor changes license metering, camera policy or ownership
a competing platform materially changes the comparison

base.update_signal: vendor terms, camera policy, ownership or the competitive platform set changes

nodes.definition: Build the per-site monthly cost stack as a set of mechanisms the operator can verify per deal, never as remembered numbers: cloud storage cost moves with resolution, frame rate, retention days and continuous-versus-event recording; the platform license moves with camera count and feature tier; support labor is a probabilistic cost (expected tickets and truck rolls per site per year times loaded labor rate); billing and payment processing take their percentage; and a reserve accrues for warranty swaps and re-terminations. The stack exists so every quoted subscription has a computed floor under it: each driver is listed with what moves it, which sibling-discipline design choice sets it (the retention promise, the camera count), and how it is price-checked against current vendor rate cards before quoting.

included: storage, license, labor, billing and reserve drivers
excluded: the bandwidth and storage engineering math itself
asserting current vendor rates as fact

pros.claim: A driver-by-driver cost stack shows a non-accountant exactly why a 12-camera 30-day site costs more to serve than a 4-camera 7-day site
pros.example: doubling a promised retention window appears as a computed storage line in the stack, not as a gut feel about cloud costs

cons.claim: Cost stacks built once and never refreshed quietly rot as vendor rate cards change
cons.example: a platform license increase absorbed for a year because quotes still used last year's stack

failure_modes: quoting from a competitor's rumored price instead of the operator's own computed floor
omitting support labor and truck-roll reserve so high-touch sites are served at a loss
acceptance_tests: the stack lists every monthly cost driver with its mechanism, its current verification source (vendor rate card, labor log) and the date it was last checked
revisit_triggers: any vendor rate card or cloud storage pricing changes
support-ticket logs show actual labor cost diverging from the stack's assumption

base.update_signal: a vendor rate card, storage price or observed support-labor cost moves

nodes.definition: Design the tier ladder that turns one service into a choice: a small set (three at launch) of good-better-best packages whose differentiators are things buyers feel - retention window length, event-only versus continuous cloud recording, cameras included before a per-camera add-on, support level (business-hours remote versus priority with a truck-roll response), and whether footage-retrieval help for incidents is included or billed per use. The ladder is built so the middle tier is the intended home for the beachhead segment, the bottom tier is a real product rather than bait, and every differentiator is deliverable on the chosen platform; retention and access promises appear on the tier sheet itself because they are product, not fine print.

pros.claim: A three-tier ladder converts a price argument into a package choice and lifts average revenue without pressure tactics
pros.example: a restaurant owner offered 7, 30 and 60-day retention tiers argues about which window fits an insurance claim, not about whether to pay monthly

cons.claim: Tiers multiply faster than they are pruned, and each variant adds quoting, provisioning and support permutations
cons.example: six overlapping packages after a year of one-off exceptions makes every new quote a negotiation again

failure_modes: differentiating tiers on internal jargon buyers cannot feel
promising a tier feature such as analytics that the chosen platform cannot deliver
acceptance_tests: the tier sheet shows at most three launch tiers, each stating retention days, recording mode, included cameras, support level and retrieval help, all verified against platform capability
revisit_triggers: win/loss or pilot data shows buyers clustering in the wrong tier or demanding a missing differentiator
the platform adds or removes tier-relevant features

base.update_signal: buyer tier-selection behavior or platform capability changes the ladder's assumptions

nodes.definition: Choose where the business earns: mark up cameras and switches like a dealer, or pass hardware near cost and earn on the subscription. Hold it as a mechanism, not a fixed answer: hardware markup recovers cash immediately and derisks early cancellation but raises the visible entry price against hardware-store anchors; subsidizing hardware into the monthly fee lowers the entry barrier and grows the book faster but converts hardware into working capital at risk until the subsidy is recovered - which is why subsidy depth must be matched to a term commitment that covers it. Who owns the hardware (customer-owned versus operator-owned hardware-as-a-service) then determines the balance-sheet load, the end-of-life refresh obligation, and what may be repossessed or deactivated at cancellation - stated openly in the contract, never done covertly.

pros.claim: Matching subsidy depth to term commitment makes the aggressive low-entry offer financeable instead of a gamble
pros.example: a subsidized 8-camera restaurant kit tied to a term long enough to repay the kit cost keeps an early cancel from being a straight loss

cons.claim: Subsidy economics collapse quietly if churn or early cancels exceed the assumption baked into the term
cons.example: month-to-month buyers on subsidized kits who cancel in month four leave the operator holding unpaid-for hardware already on their walls

failure_modes: copying the alarm industry's deep-subsidy model without its term enforcement or capital base
mixing subsidized and markup deals ad hoc so nobody can say which deals make money
acceptance_tests: the strategy states the chosen allocation per offer, the ownership model, and the term length that must cover any subsidy, and every quote traces to one of the stated allocations
revisit_triggers: hardware costs shift materially through supply, tariffs or model end-of-life
observed early-cancel behavior diverges from the subsidy assumption

base.update_signal: hardware cost, churn behavior or capital availability moves against the chosen allocation

nodes.definition: Price the installation event by mechanism: a per-job build-up from crew-day rate, camera count, cable-run difficulty (ceiling type, masonry, conduit), height and lift needs, trenching or wireless bridges for detached yards, network tidy-up, and commissioning time - with a site-condition contingency and a deposit that filters non-serious buyers. The install price also carries strategy: it may be discounted against a longer subscription commitment, but the discount is a computed trade against future margin, not a habit, and the quote always itemizes what is one-time versus monthly so the buyer never confuses the two. The engineering scoping itself (which cameras, where) belongs to the design discipline; this unit owns turning a scoped job into a defensible price.

excluded: asserting standard install prices as fact

pros.claim: Build-up pricing survives the customer's why-so-much conversation because every line has a physical reason
pros.example: showing the trench to the yard gate as its own line item ends the comparison with a cousin's two-camera house job

cons.claim: Mechanical build-up can price the operator out of simple jobs a flat-rate competitor wins
cons.example: a straightforward 4-camera bungalow quoted with full contingency loses to a fixed-package installer

failure_modes: absorbing scope creep found on install day because the quote never reserved contingency
hiding install cost inside the monthly fee without computing the recovery term
acceptance_tests: each install quote itemizes labor, materials, difficulty factors and contingency, separates one-time from monthly, and any commitment discount shows the term that funds it
revisit_triggers: install-day variance logs show systematic under- or over-quoting for a job type
crew day-rate or lift-rental costs change

base.update_signal: install variance logs or crew cost inputs contradict the build-up assumptions

nodes.definition: Set each tier's monthly price between two computed lines: the floor - the per-site cost stack plus target margin - and the ceiling - what the site's alternative set makes credible (a DIY consumer kit with app storage, an alarm company's camera add-on, a no-recurring installer, or doing nothing), discovered through discovery conversations and win/loss, not asserted. The method is deliberately numberless in this KB: no per-camera market rate is stated as fact anywhere; the operator prices by running the floor computation on the current cost stack, testing the ceiling locally per segment, and positioning tiers inside that band with the middle tier at the beachhead's comfortable point. Discipline rules complete it: below-floor deals are walked or restructured (explicit time-boxed pilots excepted), and price moves are governance events, never per-deal improvisation.

excluded: asserting any market price as fact

pros.claim: Floor-and-ceiling discipline turns pricing from confidence theater into a repeatable computation plus a local test
pros.example: when a lean competitor undercuts, the operator checks whether the rival sits below the operator's own floor instead of panic-matching the number

cons.claim: Cost-plus floors ignore willingness-to-pay differences a value-based approach could capture
cons.example: a jeweler whose loss exposure dwarfs a cafe's may be charged the same tier price the floor logic produced

failure_modes: anchoring price on a rumored competitor number instead of the operator's own floor
quietly discounting deal by deal until the book's average sits below the floor
acceptance_tests: every tier price on the current sheet traces to a dated floor computation and a named local ceiling test, and no artifact states a specific market price as fact
revisit_triggers: the cost stack changes, which moves every floor
win/loss shows a segment's ceiling has moved

base.update_signal: a cost-stack change or win/loss ceiling evidence moves the pricing band

nodes.definition: Design the commitment: term length versus month-to-month per offer, what renewal looks like (plain-language notice before any auto-renewal - an obligation class regulated in many places, so verify current rules in your jurisdiction), what cancellation costs and requires, and - specific to this trade - what happens to footage and hardware on exit: how long stored video remains retrievable after cancellation, whether cameras keep recording locally, who owns the equipment, and any remote-deactivation policy stated openly in the contract rather than discovered by the customer. Terms exist to protect subsidy recovery and revenue predictability, not to trap: the term asked of a buyer must be explainable by the economics of their own deal.

included: cancellation and exit disposition of footage and hardware
excluded: asserting a jurisdiction's auto-renewal statute as fact

pros.claim: Terms sized to subsidy recovery make aggressive offers safe while staying explainable to the buyer
pros.example: explaining that the discounted install is funded by the term turns the commitment from a trap into visible arithmetic

cons.claim: Term requirements lengthen sales cycles and repel commitment-averse smaller buyers
cons.example: a food-truck owner who cannot predict next season refuses any multi-year paper on principle

failure_modes: auto-renewing without the notice a local consumer rule requires
exit terms that surprise the customer - footage gone same-day, cameras deactivated - and detonate local reputation
acceptance_tests: the contract template states term, renewal notice, cancellation mechanics and footage-and-hardware disposition on exit in plain language, with the auto-renewal obligation class flagged for local verification
revisit_triggers: a jurisdiction updates auto-renewal or consumer-notice rules
cancellation disputes show a term or exit clause is being misread

base.update_signal: a consumer-contract rule change or a pattern of exit disputes surfaces

nodes.definition: Make retention and access a first-class, priced element of every tier instead of an afterthought: each package states how many days of footage are kept, whether recording is continuous or event-based, who at the customer may view live versus recorded video, how footage for an incident is exported and handed over, and what the operator's own access to customer video is limited to (support diagnostics with consent, never casual viewing). The promise is designed inside two constraints: longer retention is a direct storage-cost driver (priced, not gifted), and privacy rules for video retention and employee or customer viewing vary by jurisdiction, so every retention-and-access statement carries the verify-locally flag. Operating the policy day-to-day - auditing viewers, honoring requests - belongs to the operations discipline; this unit owns promising it correctly at sale time.

included: the verify-locally flag on each promise

pros.claim: Selling retention and access explicitly converts a compliance chore into a differentiator honest buyers pay for
pros.example: a shop owner picks the 30-day tier because insurance claims there take weeks, understanding exactly what the extra monthly buys

cons.claim: Detailed promises create an audit surface the operator must then live up to
cons.example: a stated named-viewer list means an operations process must actually maintain it site by site

failure_modes: quoting retention days no one priced into the storage line
leaving the operator's own access to customer footage undefined in the offer
acceptance_tests: every tier sheet and proposal states retention days, recording mode, customer viewer roles, export handling and the operator's access limits, each carrying the verify-locally flag
revisit_triggers: storage economics change the cost of a promised window
a jurisdiction's retention or workplace-viewing rules change

base.update_signal: storage cost or a privacy-rule change alters what a tier may promise

nodes.definition: Codify how this product is sold, because surveillance sells easily on fear and that ease is the trap: the code requires disclosure-first proposals (total cost over the term, what is one-time versus monthly, what the subscription does and does not include), forbids manufactured fear (no invented local-crime statistics, no staged near-miss stories, no implying the buyer is currently being cased), forbids capability inflation (no promising face recognition, guaranteed identification or conviction-grade imagery beyond what the platform demonstrably delivers), and mandates vulnerable-consumer care - elderly or frightened buyers get plain language, explicit room to think, and no same-visit pressure close. The code is a sales-qualifying artifact: reps are trained on it, deals are reviewed against it, and it exists in writing before the first pitch, not after the first complaint.

excluded: advertising-law specifics beyond the flagged obligation class

pros.claim: Disclosure-first selling compounds into the referral engine a local recurring business lives on
pros.example: a restaurant owner walked honestly through total cost refers the whole block; one fear-pitched neighbor poisons it

cons.claim: Refusing fear and urgency tactics concedes some deals to competitors who use them
cons.example: a rival's crime-wave flyer closes a scared shopkeeper the code would have advised to compare quotes calmly

failure_modes: reps drifting into scare framing because it converts in the short term
quoting the monthly-only price while burying the term total
acceptance_tests: the written code covers disclosure-first, no-fear-claims, capability truth and vulnerable-buyer safeguards, and sales materials and pitches are reviewed against it
revisit_triggers: a deal review or complaint shows the code was bent
a new channel such as door-to-door canvassing raises fresh pressure-selling risk

base.update_signal: a complaint, deal review or new sales channel exposes a gap in the written code

nodes.definition: Qualify before quoting, on five questions: what actual loss or incident drives the inquiry (anchoring the proposal in the buyer's own facts, not fear); whether the prospect owns the property or holds the owner's written authority to mount cameras (tenant-landlord surprises kill installs); whether the stated purpose is lawful and disclosed (a buyer seeking covert monitoring of staff, a partner or a neighbor is declined per the charter); whether the site's uplink is plausibly sufficient for cloud recording (recorded as a go/no-go flag, with the engineering math left to the design discipline); and who controls budget and signature. The output is a qualification record the proposal builds on, including the declared purpose - which later bounds what the installed system may be used for.

pros.claim: Five-question qualification kills doomed deals in one conversation instead of after a wasted site visit
pros.example: learning the inquirer is a tenant mid-dispute with the landlord stops a quote that could never be installed

cons.claim: Strict qualification gates slow the pipeline in a business that needs early wins
cons.example: insisting on written landlord authority before any quote loses an impatient strip-mall prospect

failure_modes: quoting first and discovering authority or bandwidth blockers after commitment
recording no declared purpose, so covert intent is discovered only at install
acceptance_tests: every proposal links to a qualification record answering loss driver, property authority, lawful declared purpose, uplink go/no-go and budget authority
revisit_triggers: install-day surprises trace back to a qualification gap
a new segment's qualification needs exceed the five questions, e.g. multi-tenant industrial parks

base.update_signal: install-day surprises or a new segment expose a gap in the qualification set

nodes.definition: Assemble the proposal as a disclosure instrument that also sells: two or at most three configurations (not a menu of ten), each showing the itemized one-time install, the chosen tier with its retention-and-access statement, the monthly amount and the computed total over the proposed term, what support includes, and the verify-locally note on surveillance rules. The proposal reuses the qualification record's loss driver as its opening frame - this is what happened, this is the coverage that addresses it - and contains no capability the vetted platform cannot deliver, which is the gate that prevents the sold-but-impossible feature. Format discipline is the ethics made visible: nothing material lives in fine print.

included: the platform-deliverability check on every promise

pros.claim: A total-cost, option-framed proposal closes on trust and pre-empts the churn born of billing surprise
pros.example: a buyer who saw the term total on page one never opens a month-nine dispute claiming the fee was hidden

cons.claim: Full disclosure documents are longer and slower than a one-line teaser quote
cons.example: against a competitor's single low monthly headline, the honest term total can look expensive in the first minute

failure_modes: promising a feature the platform cannot ship
drowning the buyer in ten configurations that stall the decision
acceptance_tests: each proposal shows itemized install, the tier with its retention-and-access statement, monthly and term totals, support scope and the verify-locally note, in 2-3 options with every promised capability platform-verified
revisit_triggers: win/loss attributes losses to proposal length or framing
the tier sheet or contract template changes upstream

base.update_signal: win/loss evidence or an upstream tier/contract change alters the proposal format

nodes.definition: Position against the four alternatives every prospect silently holds: DIY consumer cameras (cheap, app-based, no service, weak evidence handling), the alarm company's camera add-on (bundled but generic and contract-heavy), the no-recurring local installer (cheap once, absent when footage is needed), and doing nothing. The operator's defensible ground is local accountable service plus evidence-grade outcomes: someone answers, camera health is watched, and footage of an incident is actually retrievable and exportable - claims that must be true and platform-verified, not aspirational. Positioning never leans on fear or on rubbishing the alternative a buyer already owns; it names the honest gap - what happens with that option when you actually need last Tuesday's footage - and prices the difference as service.

excluded: fear appeals and invented crime data
pricing the competitors' products as fact

pros.claim: Naming the buyer's real alternatives pre-empts the objection instead of meeting it cold
pros.example: acknowledging a doorbell camera is fine for parcels, then showing its gap for a register dispute, reframes without rubbishing

cons.claim: Positioning against DIY invites the direct price comparison the service model loses on sticker
cons.example: a spreadsheet-minded buyer totals hardware-store camera prices and calls the subscription expensive before service value registers

failure_modes: competing on hardware price against retail-boxed cameras
claiming evidence outcomes the platform's export tooling cannot actually deliver
acceptance_tests: the positioning one-pager states, per alternative, the honest gap and the operator's verifiable difference, with no fear appeals or fabricated statistics
revisit_triggers: a new credible alternative appears locally, e.g. a franchise VSaaS dealer or a markedly better DIY product
win/loss shows an alternative winning for a new reason

base.update_signal: the local alternative set or its win/loss behavior changes

nodes.definition: Keep a living per-site unit-economics view that decides deals rather than decorating slides: for each site, monthly revenue minus the cost stack yields site gross margin; the acquisition load (selling time, subsidized hardware, discounted install) divided by that margin yields payback months; margin times expected subscription life - a churn-informed band from the operator's own book, never an invented industry multiple - yields expected site value as a mechanism. The dashboard sets the thresholds a deal must clear (payback inside what the operator can finance, margin above floor) and shows the book-level truth that triggers governance: average margin drift, subsidy exposure outstanding, and concentration in one segment.

included: site margin, payback and expected-life mechanisms

pros.claim: Payback-and-margin thresholds make deal acceptance a calculation the whole team applies consistently
pros.example: a big flattering site that fails the payback test gets restructured instead of celebrated

cons.claim: Early books are too small for churn-informed life estimates, so thresholds rest on wide assumptions
cons.example: with fifteen sites on the board, one cancellation swings the expected-life band embarrassingly

failure_modes: judging deals on install revenue while subscription margin quietly sits below floor
carrying subsidy exposure invisibly until several early cancels land at once
acceptance_tests: every accepted deal shows computed site margin and payback against stated thresholds, and the book view shows margin drift and outstanding subsidy exposure
revisit_triggers: observed churn or support cost shifts the assumed life or margin
subsidy exposure approaches the financing limit

base.update_signal: observed churn, support cost or subsidy exposure moves a threshold input

nodes.definition: Land the first sites in the beachhead deliberately: pick visible, well-connected owners (the taqueria everyone knows, the contractor who runs the trade association), give them an explicit pilot agreement - time-boxed pricing, a stated conversion date to a standard tier, and the feedback they owe - rather than a quiet permanent discount, and convert their outcome into reference assets: a case story in the owner's own words, a referral ask, and site photos. Any use of camera imagery or incident footage in marketing requires the customer's written consent and de-identification of bystanders - the privacy discipline applies to the operator's own marketing first. Pilots exist to buy segment truth (real conversion, real tier fit, real objections), and their learnings are formally fed back into the segment map and tier sheet.

included: time-boxed pilot agreements with conversion dates

pros.claim: A lighthouse owner's referral collapses the trust barrier that surveillance-and-subscription selling faces cold
pros.example: the known contractor telling his suppliers the yard thefts stopped closes more yards than any flyer

cons.claim: Pilot discounts anchor early-market price expectations if conversion terms are soft
cons.example: the whole restaurant block hears the pilot's number and expects it as the street price

failure_modes: pilots on permanent handshake discounts that never convert
publishing customer footage in marketing without consent and de-identification
acceptance_tests: each pilot has a written agreement with time-boxed pricing, a conversion date and a feedback obligation, and every marketing use of site imagery has written consent with bystanders de-identified
revisit_triggers: a pilot passes its conversion date unconverted
pilot learnings contradict the segment map or tier design

base.update_signal: a pilot converts, expires or returns evidence that contradicts offer assumptions

nodes.definition: Run the offer as a governed product, on triggers rather than moods: a periodic review - and an immediate one when a trigger fires - that re-checks the cost stack against current vendor rate cards, reads win/loss and pilot evidence, prunes tiers that stopped earning their complexity, and decides price moves with the grandfathering question answered explicitly: existing subscribers keep their price for a stated period, or move with honest notice under the contract's renewal mechanics, never silently. Every reprice states its mechanism to customers in plain terms - storage costs rose, so the 60-day tier changes at your renewal with notice - because a surveillance subscription lives on trust and a stealthy increase spends it. Changes version the tier sheet so sales, installs in flight and operations always know which offer a site is on.

pros.claim: Trigger-driven governance catches margin rot early while changes are small and explainable
pros.example: a platform license increase surfaces at the next review as a modest, noticed reprice instead of a year-late emergency

cons.claim: Governance cadence adds overhead a small operator is tempted to skip while selling is going well
cons.example: review meetings feel bureaucratic in month six, right before the first vendor price change lands unnoticed

failure_modes: repricing new deals while the legacy book silently erodes below floor
springing increases on subscribers without the contract's notice
acceptance_tests: each review is dated and records the cost-stack re-check, win/loss reading, tier prune decision and any reprice with its grandfathering and notice plan, and the tier sheet is versioned
revisit_triggers: a trigger fires between reviews - vendor reprice, storage cost move, churn spike
a reprice draws disproportionate cancellations

base.update_signal: a governance trigger fires or a reprice produces unexpected cancellation behavior

nodes.definition: Define what a closed deal must hand to the two sibling disciplines before anyone schedules a ladder: to system design - the qualification record (declared lawful purpose, property authority, uplink go/no-go), the sold camera-count assumption and coverage intent, the tier's retention and recording-mode promise, and any site constraints sales observed; to service operations - the tier and support level sold, the retention-and-access policy promised, the named customer viewer roles, and the contract's term, renewal and exit mechanics. The handoff is a gate with a definition-of-done: design may reject a package that under-specifies, forcing sales to complete it rather than exporting surprises to install day, and nothing in the package may exceed what the proposal actually promised - the sold-versus-buildable check running one last time.

included: the handoff package contents for design and for operations

pros.claim: A rejectable handoff package makes sales complete its own work instead of exporting gaps to the install crew
pros.example: design bouncing a deal with no landlord authority letter costs a day, versus a crew on site being turned away at the door

cons.claim: A strict gate adds friction and paper between closing and installing, when speed impresses customers
cons.example: a same-week install promise dies in checklist review over one trivially incomplete field

failure_modes: deals sliding straight to scheduling with no uplink flag or authority document
operations discovering at the first incident that sales promised retrieval help the sold tier does not include
acceptance_tests: no deal schedules until the handoff package carries the qualification record, coverage and retention promises, tier and support level, viewer roles and contract mechanics, and design/ops sign acceptance or bounce with named gaps
revisit_triggers: install-day or first-incident surprises trace to a package field
the design or operations intake contract changes

base.update_signal: a downstream surprise or an intake-contract change exposes a missing package field

edges.why_related: segments are mapped against the outcome and revenue model the thesis fixes
the buy-or-build decision serves the subscription book the thesis commits to
tiers package the exact outcome and revenue events the thesis defines
positioning defends the outcome-plus-subscription framing the thesis stakes out
the beachhead is chosen from the mapped segments' repeatability, density and referral structure
qualification scripts specialize on each mapped segment's loss profile and decision-maker
vendor diligence executes the platform route the decision selects
the chosen route determines whether a platform license or own-infrastructure cost sits in the stack
the cost stack computes the floor every monthly price must clear
subsidy depth is judged against the recurring margin the stack says each site yields
install quotes draw labor, materials and contingency mechanics from the same verified cost base
prices are set per tier, so the ladder must exist before the numbers
each tier's retention and access statement is written into the ladder it belongs to
term and renewal paper is drafted around the tiers it commits buyers to
any subsidy recovered through the monthly fee changes what the subscription price must carry
the itemized install build-up is the one-time half of every proposal
tier prices and computed term totals populate the proposal's disclosure
the retention-and-access statement is a mandatory proposal section
site margin and payback are computed from the priced subscription
the handoff package is assembled from what the accepted proposal promised
operations receives the term, renewal and exit mechanics the contract fixed
pilots are landed inside the chosen beachhead to buy segment truth
governance reviews fire on the margin drift and subsidy exposure the dashboard surfaces
qualification must capture the declared lawful purpose and decline covert-intent buyers per the charter
retention and viewing promises must fit the jurisdiction-varying privacy classes and carry the verify-locally flag
proposals must lead with total-cost disclosure and contain no fear framing or unverified capability claims
renewal and exit clauses must satisfy the code's disclosure-first bar, not merely local minimums
reference and marketing use of customer sites and imagery requires written consent and de-identification
recovering hardware in the monthly fee pushes the subscription toward the segment's ceiling while upfront markup inflates the entry price
edges.resolution_rule: match the allocation to the deal's term: subsidize into the monthly only when a committed term covers the subsidy; for month-to-month buyers recover hardware upfront and keep the subscription at the tier price

edges.why_related: fear and urgency framing wins surveillance deals short-term, and positioning is where that temptation concentrates
edges.resolution_rule: the selling code wins unconditionally: positioning may name honest gaps in alternatives but never manufactured fear, invented crime data or capability inflation; a pitch that needs fear is rewritten or the deal is left

edges.why_related: each segment pulls the ladder toward custom packages while the ladder needs few standard tiers to stay quotable and supportable
edges.resolution_rule: hold one standard ladder with bounded per-segment add-ons; a segment earns a dedicated tier only after repeated proven demand recorded at the governance review

edges.why_related: the platform license visibly drags every site's margin, tempting a premature own-stack jump the dashboard appears to justify
edges.resolution_rule: stay on the platform until subscribed volume and engineering capacity clear the modeled crossover with migration cost included; the dashboard triggers a re-decision memo, never an impulsive replatform

edges.why_related: pilots need easy low-commitment entry while term design exists to secure commitment and subsidy recovery
edges.resolution_rule: pilots run on explicit time-boxed pilot agreements with a stated conversion date; standard term paper is never silently discounted, and unconverted pilots end rather than roll on

edges.why_related: every promised retention day and continuous-recording commitment flows directly into the storage line of the cost stack
the credibility of the local alternative set is what sets the value ceiling the monthly price must sit under
no proposal is assembled until the qualification record - authority, purpose, uplink, budget - exists to build on
tier differentiators are committed only after vendor diligence confirms the platform actually delivers them
margin drift or payback misses on the dashboard send pricing back through the floor-and-ceiling method
pilot conversion, objections and tier fit flow back to correct the segment map's assumptions
both allocate one-time revenue against recurring margin - the install discount and the hardware subsidy are the same trade wearing different clothes

conflict_axes.name: hardware_upfront_vs_subscription_margin
conflict_axes.description: Recovering hardware cost upfront derisks cancellation but raises the entry price; subsidizing it into the monthly grows the book while piling working capital at risk.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: match subsidy depth to a term commitment that covers it, and never mix the two allocations invisibly across deals

conflict_axes.name: platform_speed_vs_ownstack_control
conflict_axes.description: A white-label VSaaS platform launches the business in weeks but takes a license from every subscription forever; an own stack keeps the margin but buys engineering and on-call liability.
poles: launch fast on a vendor platform
control the whole margin on an own stack
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: start on the platform, model the crossover with migration cost included, and re-decide at volume thresholds, not by annual habit

conflict_axes.name: deterrence_truth_vs_fear_closing
conflict_axes.description: Surveillance closes fastest on fear, but fear-selling breaches the code, invites regulatory and reputational blowback, and poisons the referral economy a local operator lives on.
poles: close on manufactured fear and urgency
sell on disclosed outcomes and the buyer's own facts
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: the ethical selling code dominates: anchor pitches in the prospect's actual loss driver and verifiable service outcomes, never invented crime data

conflict_axes.name: tier_simplicity_vs_segment_fit
conflict_axes.description: Five segments each pull the ladder toward custom packages, while quoting, provisioning and support all get cheaper the fewer standard tiers exist.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: keep three standard tiers with bounded per-segment add-ons and let governance promote a custom tier only on repeated proven demand

conflict_axes.name: retention_promise_vs_storage_cost
conflict_axes.description: Longer retention windows and continuous recording sell tiers and serve insurance timelines, but every promised day is a storage cost the subscription must carry.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: price retention explicitly per tier from the cost stack and sell longer windows as a paid upgrade, never as a free concession

conflict_axes.name: commitment_security_vs_buyer_flexibility
conflict_axes.description: Term contracts secure subsidy recovery and predictable revenue, while month-to-month terms win trust-driven and commitment-averse buyers.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: offer both honestly: terms priced to fund subsidies, month-to-month priced with hardware recovered upfront, each explainable by its own economics

conflict_axes.name: price_floor_discipline_vs_deal_hunger
conflict_axes.description: A young operator needs wins and is tempted below the computed floor, but every below-floor site loses money each month for the life of its subscription.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: hold the floor, restructure the deal (fewer cameras, shorter retention, different tier) instead of discounting, and time-box any pilot exception

conflict_axes.name: beachhead_focus_vs_segment_breadth
conflict_axes.description: Focusing on one or two segments compounds referrals and standardizes installs, while breadth catches more inbound revenue but standardizes nothing.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: lead with the beachhead, take opportunistic off-segment deals only at standard terms, and defer segments explicitly rather than serving them badly

conflict_axes.name: sales_promise_vs_deliverable_scope
conflict_axes.description: Proposals close faster the more they promise, while design and operations can only deliver what the vetted platform and the sold tier actually contain.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: run the sold-versus-buildable check at proposal time and again at handoff, and let design bounce under-specified or over-promised packages

conflict_axes.name: legal_variance_vs_offer_standardization
conflict_axes.description: One standardized offer scales, but video privacy, audio consent and camera-placement rules differ by jurisdiction, so a standard promise can be lawful on one street and not another.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: standardize the mechanism and flag every legally-sensitive promise verify-locally, adapting the offer text where a served jurisdiction's rules demand it

edge_cases.description: A buyer asks for hidden cameras to watch employees without telling them
edge_cases.trigger: covert-monitoring intent surfaces during discovery or in a written request
edge_cases.mitigation: decline with the scripted refusal, record the declined purpose, and offer only disclosed-surveillance alternatives if the buyer accepts disclosure

edge_cases.description: A tenant wants cameras mounted on a building the landlord owns
edge_cases.trigger: property authority is missing or disputed at qualification
edge_cases.mitigation: require the owner's written authorization before any proposal, and scope removable, tenant-owned mounting options where the landlord limits penetrations

edge_cases.description: An elderly homeowner, frightened by a neighborhood rumor, asks to sign for the top tier on the spot
edge_cases.trigger: a vulnerable buyer under fear pressure reaches for the most expensive package same-visit
edge_cases.mitigation: apply the vulnerable-consumer safeguards: plain-language total cost, a fit-for-need tier recommendation, explicit room to think, and no same-visit close

edge_cases.description: A restaurant owner wants audio recording on every camera to settle staff disputes
edge_cases.trigger: an audio-capture request lands where consent rules are typically stricter than video
edge_cases.mitigation: keep audio off by default, flag the audio-consent obligation class for local verification, and quote audio only after the local check clears it

edge_cases.description: The VSaaS vendor raises its per-camera license mid-year, squeezing margin across the whole book
edge_cases.trigger: a vendor rate-card change lands between governance reviews
edge_cases.mitigation: fire an immediate governance review: rebuild the cost stack, decide the reprice with grandfathering and notice, and re-check the vendor against its walk-away conditions

edge_cases.description: A prospect demands a months-long continuous-recording retention window at the bottom-tier price
edge_cases.trigger: a retention request far outside the tier ladder arrives during quoting
edge_cases.mitigation: quote it as a custom line showing the storage-driver mechanism that prices it, rather than discounting the promise into an existing tier

edge_cases.description: After signing, the site's uplink proves too weak for the promised cloud recording mode
edge_cases.trigger: the qualification uplink flag was skipped or waved through
edge_cases.mitigation: make the uplink go/no-go a mandatory handoff field design may bounce, and re-scope the sold recording mode with the customer before install rather than after

edge_cases.description: A buyer anchors on hardware-store camera prices and calls the subscription a rip-off
edge_cases.trigger: a DIY price anchor dominates the sales conversation
edge_cases.mitigation: concede what DIY does well, reframe on the service gap - retrieval, health monitoring, accountable support - and never chase the hardware sticker below the floor

edge_cases.description: A pilot restaurant expects its discounted pilot price to continue forever
edge_cases.trigger: a pilot reaches its conversion date with soft or unwritten terms
edge_cases.mitigation: put the conversion date and standard-tier landing in the written pilot agreement up front, and end unconverted pilots rather than rolling the discount

edge_cases.description: A contractor's job-site subscription outlives the job when the site closes in eight months
edge_cases.trigger: a per-site subscription is sold to an inherently temporary site
edge_cases.mitigation: sell the contractor segment a relocatable site subscription whose term follows the account, moving cameras to the next yard instead of cancelling

edge_cases.description: A signed proposal promises license-plate analytics the chosen platform does not offer
edge_cases.trigger: the sold-versus-buildable check was skipped at proposal time
edge_cases.mitigation: catch it at the handoff gate, renegotiate honestly with the customer before install, and add the missing capability to the vendor-diligence watch list

edge_cases.description: A prospect asks the operator to state how much crime the cameras will prevent
edge_cases.trigger: the buyer requests a quantified deterrence guarantee
edge_cases.mitigation: describe deterrence and evidence value qualitatively with the buyer's own loss driver, decline to invent a statistic, and put no quantified crime claim in writing

workflow.description: Fix the outcome sold, the install-plus-subscription revenue model and the subscription book as the asset
workflow.gate: outcome, both revenue events, the compounding-book claim and the lawful-purpose commitment are stated

workflow.description: Write the disclosed-purpose rule, covert-use refusal script, obligation classes and verify-locally flag
workflow.gate: the charter names the obligation classes, the audio-off default and the verify-locally flag, and the refusal script exists

workflow.action: Map segments and pick the beachhead
workflow.description: Profile the five segments' losses, triggers and fee tolerance, then choose 1-2 lead segments on repeatability, density and referrals
workflow.gate: every segment carries loss profile, trigger, decision-maker, camera band and fee tolerance, and the beachhead choice states its evidence

workflow.description: Choose the cloud route on volume, engineering and capital mechanisms with crossover conditions
workflow.gate: the memo records the route, the mechanism behind it and the re-evaluation conditions

workflow.description: Verify license metering, white-label depth, camera openness, exit portability and vendor stability
workflow.gate: all five diligence questions are answered with evidence and walk-away conditions are named

workflow.description: List every monthly cost driver with its mechanism and its per-deal verification source
workflow.gate: each driver shows what moves it, its verification source and its last-checked date

workflow.action: Design the tier ladder with retention and access as product
workflow.description: Build three launch tiers on buyer-felt differentiators, embedding each tier's retention-and-access statement
workflow.gate: at most three tiers, each stating retention, recording mode, cameras, support and retrieval help, all platform-verified

workflow.action: Set hardware, install and subscription pricing
workflow.description: Choose the hardware-margin allocation, build install quotes by mechanism, and place tier prices between floor and locally-tested ceiling
workflow.gate: every price traces to a dated floor computation and a named ceiling test, and any subsidy shows its covering term

workflow.action: Design contract terms, renewal and exit
workflow.description: Fix term structures, renewal notice, cancellation mechanics and footage-and-hardware disposition on exit
workflow.gate: term, renewal notice, cancellation and exit disposition are stated plainly with the auto-renewal class flagged verify-locally

workflow.action: Codify the ethical selling code and qualification script
workflow.description: Write the disclosure-first code with its prohibitions and safeguards, and the five-question qualification script that enforces the charter
workflow.artifact: written selling code plus qualification checklist
workflow.gate: disclosure-first, no-fear, capability-truth and vulnerable-buyer rules exist in writing with the covert-intent decline scripted

workflow.description: Build the 2-3 option proposal template with itemized install, tier statements, term totals and the verify-locally note
workflow.gate: the template shows one-time versus monthly, term totals, retention-and-access statements and only platform-verified capabilities

workflow.action: Stand up pilots, unit economics and the handoff gate
workflow.description: Launch time-boxed beachhead pilots, wire the per-site economics thresholds, and enforce the rejectable handoff package to design and operations
workflow.artifact: pilot agreements, unit-economics dashboard and handoff checklist
workflow.gate: pilots carry conversion dates, deals clear margin and payback thresholds, and no deal schedules without a complete accepted handoff package

dominance_rules.rule: Lawful, disclosed surveillance dominates any revenue opportunity
dominance_rules.rationale: one covert or unlawful installation can end the operator's license to operate and outweighs any deal
dominance_rules.trigger: a request implies covert monitoring, undisclosed audio or unlawful camera placement
dominance_rules.action: decline with the scripted refusal and record the declined purpose

dominance_rules.rule: The verify-locally flag dominates offer standardization
dominance_rules.rationale: video, audio and placement rules differ sharply by jurisdiction, so a standard promise can be unlawful next door
dominance_rules.trigger: a legally-sensitive promise (retention, audio, viewing, auto-renewal) enters an offer or proposal
dominance_rules.action: attach the verify-current-rules-in-your-jurisdiction flag and adapt the promise where the local check requires

dominance_rules.rule: The computed cost floor dominates deal hunger
dominance_rules.rationale: a below-floor subscription loses money every month for the life of the site
dominance_rules.trigger: a deal prices below the floor for any reason other than an explicit time-boxed pilot
dominance_rules.action: walk or restructure the package (cameras, retention, tier) instead of discounting below floor

dominance_rules.rule: The ethical selling code dominates closing technique
dominance_rules.rationale: fear-selling converts today and destroys the referral economy and reputation the book depends on
dominance_rules.trigger: a pitch, flyer or proposal leans on manufactured fear, urgency or invented statistics
dominance_rules.action: rewrite it around the buyer's own loss driver and verifiable outcomes, or drop the pitch

dominance_rules.rationale: retention and access policy is a first-class design decision, not fine print discovered after signature
dominance_rules.trigger: a proposal or tier sheet omits retention days, viewer roles or the operator's access limits
dominance_rules.action: block the proposal until the retention-and-access statement is complete on its face

dominance_rules.rationale: a sold-but-impossible feature becomes a broken contract and a churned site
dominance_rules.trigger: a proposal names a capability not confirmed on the vendor diligence sheet
dominance_rules.action: remove or verify the capability before the proposal goes out; at handoff, bounce it

dominance_rules.rationale: invented per-camera prices, multiples or crime statistics stated as fact poison decisions and breach the content rules
dominance_rules.trigger: any artifact asserts a specific market price, account multiple or crime figure as fact
dominance_rules.action: replace the number with the mechanism or qualitative band plus its per-deal local verification path

dominance_rules.rule: Subsidy-term matching dominates the low-entry-price urge
dominance_rules.rationale: unmatched subsidies convert growth into uncollected hardware losses at the first cancel wave
dominance_rules.trigger: a subsidized-hardware offer is proposed without a term that covers the subsidy
dominance_rules.action: restructure to a covering term or switch the deal to upfront hardware recovery

dominance_rules.rationale: an incomplete package exports sales gaps to install crews and service operations at higher cost
dominance_rules.trigger: a closed deal reaches scheduling with handoff fields missing
dominance_rules.action: hold scheduling until design and operations accept the completed package or bounce it with named gaps

anti_rework_rules.rule: Decide platform versus own stack before designing tiers
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a tier ladder promising features the eventually-chosen platform cannot deliver, forcing a redesign

anti_rework_rules.rule: Build the cost stack before setting any price
anti_rework_rules.prevents: repricing the whole book after margin surprises reveal the floor was never computed

anti_rework_rules.rule: Fix each tier's retention-and-access statement before quoting it
anti_rework_rules.prevents: renegotiating storage promises deal by deal once the cost of the promised window lands

anti_rework_rules.rule: Qualify property authority, declared purpose and uplink before proposing
anti_rework_rules.prevents: dead deals, unlawful installs and post-sale recording-mode redesigns discovered on install day

anti_rework_rules.rule: Choose the hardware-margin allocation together with the contract term
anti_rework_rules.prevents: subsidy losses on early cancels when the term never covered the hardware gap

anti_rework_rules.rule: Write the ethical selling code before the first sales conversation
anti_rework_rules.prevents: un-training fear-based habits and repairing a poisoned local reputation later

anti_rework_rules.rule: Put the conversion date in the pilot agreement before discounting anything
anti_rework_rules.prevents: permanent grandfathered pilot discounts that anchor the street price

anti_rework_rules.rule: Vet vendor exit portability before white-labeling
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a forced replatform with no export path that means touching every customer site

anti_rework_rules.rule: Define the design-and-operations handoff package before scaling sales
anti_rework_rules.prevents: install-crew rework and service surprises from deals sold on unstated assumptions

iteration_protocol.trigger: a platform license or cloud storage price changes
iteration_protocol.action: rebuild the cost stack, recompute every floor, and run a governance review with the grandfathering question answered

iteration_protocol.trigger: win/loss review shows systematic price objections or suspiciously easy wins in a segment
iteration_protocol.action: re-test that segment's value ceiling locally and reposition the tiers inside the refreshed band

iteration_protocol.trigger: cancellation or dispute patterns from the service book implicate a term, exit or tier clause
iteration_protocol.action: revise the contract template and tier ladder and version the tier sheet

iteration_protocol.trigger: a served jurisdiction changes its video, audio-consent or auto-renewal rules
iteration_protocol.action: re-check the charter, retention-and-access statements and proposal language, and re-issue affected templates

iteration_protocol.trigger: a pilot converts, expires or returns findings
iteration_protocol.action: fold the conversion, objection and tier-fit evidence back into the segment map and tier design

iteration_protocol.trigger: subscribed-camera volume approaches the modeled own-stack crossover band
iteration_protocol.action: re-run the platform decision with current volume, engineering capacity and migration cost

iteration_protocol.trigger: install crews or operations report recurring surprises traced to sold deals
iteration_protocol.action: tighten the qualification questions and the handoff package's definition-of-done

iteration_protocol.trigger: hardware cost or supply shifts through tariffs, shortages or model end-of-life
iteration_protocol.action: revisit the hardware-margin allocation and the install build-up rates

priority_rationale: The frame nodes (offer thesis and lawful-surveillance charter) come first because every segment, platform, pricing and selling choice inherits their outcome definition and legal boundary; the platform decision and cost stack must precede tiers and prices because tiers may only promise what the platform delivers and prices may only sit on a computed floor; the selling, contract and proposal nodes then package those economics honestly; and pilots, unit economics, governance and the handoff gate come last because they measure, correct and transmit the offer into design and operations.
